chapters.title: Chapter 5: Where Kelly Breaks Down, and Putting It Together

lessons.title: Alternatives to Kelly: Fixed Fractional Sizing and Volatility Targeting

children.text: Every Kelly calculation in this course needed an estimate of edge, whether p and b or μ. Chapter 3 spent an entire lesson on how unreliable that estimate usually is. Some practitioners respond by sidestepping the problem: sizing rules that never try to estimate edge at all. This lesson covers the two most common, and shows honestly where each one is stronger and weaker than Kelly.

Risk the same fixed percentage of capital on every trade, commonly 1% or 2%, regardless of how strong the specific edge is believed to be. This is the most widely taught retail risk rule for a reason: it needs no win-rate estimate, no payoff-ratio estimate, nothing beyond a stop-loss distance and a constant percentage. It is immune to the entire estimation-error problem from Lesson 3.3, because it never uses an edge estimate to begin with.
That immunity is also its weakness. A blanket rule cannot tell a great edge from a mediocre one.

body.caption: The same 2% fixed-fractional rule, three very different true edges

body.text: The identical 2% rule leaves the two strong systems trading at under 10% of their true Kelly fraction, arguably too conservative, while the weak-edge system runs at two-thirds of its full Kelly, arguably far too aggressive for how little edge actually supports it. Fixed fractional sizing treats edge size as invisible; it protects against a bad estimate by refusing to use an estimate, at the cost of never adapting to how good or weak the real opportunity actually is.

children.text: Size a position so its contribution to portfolio volatility stays roughly constant, without ever estimating expected return. This is standard practice at many systematic and managed-futures funds.

body.caption: Position weight scales inversely with the asset's own volatility, with no return estimate involved

body.text: It's tempting to think of this as "Kelly without the hard-to-estimate μ," but the two formulas scale with volatility differently, not just missing one input. Kelly's f* = μ/σ² scales with 1/σ², quadratically. Volatility targeting's w = target/σ scales with 1/σ, only linearly. The two agree only under a specific hidden assumption: that the Sharpe ratio, μ/σ, stays constant as volatility changes. If Sharpe ratio actually shifts with the volatility regime, and it usually does, the two methods diverge.

children.text: Compare a normal market regime to a crisis regime where expected returns don't just get smaller, they actually turn negative, using a 15% volatility target.

body.caption: Kelly vs volatility targeting, normal regime vs crisis

body.text: In the crisis regime, Kelly says exit the long position entirely and, if shorting were available, take a short position instead, because it uses μ and knows expected return has turned negative. Volatility targeting says stay long at 37.5%, simply smaller than before, because it never looks at direction at all, only at how much volatility has risen. Volatility targeting manages how much risk is taken; it says nothing about whether that risk still points the right way.

body.title: Compute a vol-target weight
body.prompt: Using a 12% target volatility and an asset with 30% current volatility, what position weight does volatility targeting suggest?
body.explanation: w = 12% ÷ 30% = 0.40, or 40%. Notice this calculation never used any estimate of expected return.

body.title: Choose which signal to trust
body.scenario: During a sharp market downturn, a trader following volatility targeting is holding a smaller, but still long, position, exactly as the crisis row above describes. A separate Kelly-based estimate of μ, updated with the latest data, suggests expected returns have turned negative for now.
body.prompt: Should the trader trust the volatility-targeting signal, the Kelly-based μ estimate, or neither on its own? Explain your reasoning.
body.modelAnswer: Neither fully on its own. The volatility-targeting signal is reliably measured, since realized volatility is comparatively easy to observe, but it is structurally blind to direction and will never itself suggest reducing to zero or going short. The Kelly-based μ estimate captures direction, which volatility targeting misses entirely, but μ is exactly the input Lesson 3.3 flagged as the hardest to estimate reliably, and a crisis is precisely when return estimates are least trustworthy. The more defensible approach is to treat a deteriorating μ estimate as a genuine signal to reduce further below what volatility targeting alone suggests, while remaining skeptical of how precisely that μ estimate can really be trusted in the middle of a crisis.

body.title: The scaling-law distinction
body.question: If volatility doubles, how does volatility targeting's position weight change, compared to Kelly's f*?
options: Both fall to a quarter of their original value
Volatility targeting's weight halves; Kelly's f* falls to a quarter
Both halve, since they both depend on volatility the same way
Volatility targeting's weight is unaffected; only Kelly's f* changes
body.explanation: w = target/σ scales with 1/σ, so doubling σ halves w. f* = μ/σ² scales with 1/σ², so doubling σ cuts f* to a quarter, exactly as Lesson 5.1's volatility-doubling rule showed. The two methods are not interchangeable simplifications of each other; they respond to volatility at different rates.

children.text: None of this makes Kelly the wrong tool; it makes Kelly a tool that is only as good as its μ input. A common, practical compromise: use Kelly-informed sizing where an edge has been carefully validated, exactly as this course has built up through Chapters 1 to 4, but cap the result at whatever volatility targeting or fixed fractional sizing alone would allow, whichever is smaller. This keeps the benefit of sizing that adapts to genuine edge, while putting a floor under how badly a single overconfident μ estimate can distort the outcome.

body.caption: Three sizing methods, side by side

cells: Not directly; often set via a stop distance, e.g. a multiple of ATR

points: Fixed fractional sizing avoids the estimation-error problem entirely by never using an edge estimate, at the cost of treating a strong edge and a weak edge identically.
Volatility targeting scales exposure with 1/σ, not 1/σ², and is not simply "Kelly without μ"; it agrees with Kelly only if the Sharpe ratio stays constant as volatility changes.
Volatility targeting is blind to direction: in a crisis where expected returns turn negative, it can still recommend a smaller long position, while Kelly, using μ, would say to exit or go short.

A common practical compromise caps Kelly-informed sizing at whatever a simpler, μ-free method would allow, combining Kelly's adaptiveness with the robustness of a rule that doesn't depend on the hardest input to estimate.
None of these methods is universally correct; each makes a different trade-off between adapting to genuine edge and staying robust to a wrong estimate.
